text: On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this song:
When the leaders took the lead in Israel, when the people willingly offered themselves — bless the LORD!
Hear this, you kings; listen, you rulers! I will sing to the LORD, I myself will sing; I will make music to the LORD, the God of Israel.
LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the fields of Edom, the earth shook, the heavens poured, the clouds poured down water.
The mountains melted before the LORD, even Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel.

versions.text: The mountains melted before the LORD, before the LORD, the God of Israel — that One of Sinai.
versions.explanation: The phrase זֶה סִינַי stands between the two occurrences of "before the LORD" and most naturally functions as an emphatic apposition to "the mountains" ("even Sinai"). Moving it to the end as a divine title ("that One of Sinai") both rearranges the poetic line and imports an interpretive epithet not clearly present. Restoring the Hebrew order also reads more smoothly aloud.

text: In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways lay empty, and travelers kept to the winding trails.
Village life in Israel ceased — it ceased — until I, Deborah, arose, until I arose, a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods; then war came to the gates. Was a shield to be seen, or a spear, among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel, to the people who willingly offered themselves — bless the LORD!
You who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on saddle blankets, you who walk the roads — tell of it!

To the sound of singing at the watering places, there they recount the righteous deeds of the LORD, the righteous deeds of his villagers in Israel. Then the people of the LORD marched down to the gates.
Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break into song! Rise up, Barak, and lead away your captives, son of Abinoam!
Then those who were left came down against the nobles; the people of the LORD came down for me against the mighty.

versions.text: Then those who were left came down against the nobles; the people of the LORD came down to me against the mighty.
versions.explanation: The preposition לִי here expresses benefit or advantage ("for me"), not direction toward a person; "came down to me" wrongly suggests movement toward Deborah. "For me" is both more accurate and clearer when read aloud.

text: From Ephraim they came, whose roots are in Amalek; behind you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen. From Machir the commanders came down, and from Zebulun those who bear the marshal's staff.

versions.text: From Ephraim they came, whose roots are in Amalek; behind you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen. From Machir the commanders came down, and from Zebulun those who bear the ruler's staff.
versions.explanation: סֹפֵר denotes a scribe or muster-officer (marshal) rather than a ruler; the staff belongs to the one who musters the troops, which fits the military context of the song. "Marshal's staff" also avoids confusion with the "commanders" mentioned in the previous line.

text: The princes of Issachar were with Deborah; Issachar followed Barak, rushing into the valley at his heels. But among the clans of Reuben there was deep searching of heart.
Why did you linger among the sheepfolds, listening to the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there was deep searching of heart.
Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan. And Dan — why did he linger by the ships? Asher sat still on the seacoast and remained in his harbors.
But Zebulun was a people who risked their lives to the death, and Naphtali too, on the heights of the field.
Kings came and fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo — but they carried off no silver, no plunder.
From the heavens they fought; the stars from their courses fought against Sisera.

versions.text: From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two parallel clauses, each with its own verb נִלְחָמוּ: "From heaven they fought" / "the stars from their courses fought against Sisera." The current rendering supplies "the stars" in the first line and reduces the second to a pronoun, flattening the deliberate parallelism of the war-song.

text: The river Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. March on, my soul, in strength!
Then the hooves of the horses hammered the ground — the galloping, galloping of his stallions.
"Curse Meroz," said the angel of the LORD, "bitterly curse its people, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty."
Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; most blessed of women who dwell in tents.
He asked for water; she gave him milk. In a bowl fit for a prince she brought him curds.
Her hand reached for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman's hammer. She struck Sisera, she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.
At her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still. At her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell — dead.
Through the window Sisera's mother looked out; behind the lattice she wailed: "Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why is the clatter of his chariots delayed?"
The wisest of her ladies answer her; she keeps repeating the words to herself:
"Surely they are finding and dividing the spoil — a girl or two for every man, dyed cloth as spoil for Sisera, dyed cloth richly embroidered, two embroidered pieces for the neck of the plunderer."
So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love you be like the sun when it rises in its strength. And the land had rest for forty years.
